vulcan.title: Vulcan 2022 magnetotelluric survey, South Australia: smooth 3-D electrical resistivity model
vulcan.snapshot: A three-dimensional electrical resistivity model of the Vulcan iron-oxide copper-gold (IOCG) prospect, about 30 km north-east of Olympic Dam, South Australia, from inversion of broadband magnetotelluric (MT) impedances at 98 sites on a 1 km grid. The inversion used the CGG RLM-3D code with a smoothness constraint, starting from a uniform 100 ohm.m half-space. The model images conductive sedimentary cover about 850 m thick, a low-resistivity zone beneath the cover, and a deeper, vertically extensive conductor. It is the "smooth" model of Kay et al. (2024). The companion "tear" model is Model 2 (10.25914/htcq-3537).
vulcan.overview:
Abstract

A three-dimensional electrical resistivity model of the Vulcan iron-oxide copper-gold (IOCG) prospect, about 30 km north-east of Olympic Dam, South Australia, from inversion of broadband magnetotelluric (MT) impedances at 98 sites on a 1 km grid. The inversion used the CGG RLM-3D code with a smoothness constraint, starting from a uniform 100 ohm.m half-space. The model images conductive sedimentary cover about 850 m thick, a low-resistivity zone beneath the cover, and a deeper, vertically extensive conductor. It is the "smooth" model of Kay et al. (2024). The companion "tear" model is Model 2 (10.25914/htcq-3537).

This folder holds the model, the data and settings it was computed from, and its responses and misfit. The inversion code is commercial and not included.

Known limits

1. DATA FRAME. The sensors were laid out on geomagnetic north, which is
   about 6.5 degrees east of true north and 7.5 degrees east of UTM grid
   north (the mesh axes). For this model the impedances were turned 7
   degrees towards west as a declination correction and labelled ZROT = 353.
   That label is understood to have cancelled the correction in the
   inversion, so the data were fitted about 7.5 degrees from their true
   orientation, and strike directions in the model may be turned by about
   that much towards west. Site positions are correct.

2. UBC FILES. The .msh file ends with an extra line, the mesh rotation
   (0.2 degrees), which is not part of the UBC format. Read without it, the
   model sits up to 320 m from its true position. Use the .out, .vtk or .xyzv file
   for positions.

3. MISFIT. The nRMS (0.96) depends on the error floors and cannot be
   compared with Model 2, which used different floors, frequencies and
   sites. The inversion stopped at its iteration limit.

4. STATIC LEVEL. The distortion matrices are not constrained to a mean of
   one, so model resistivities may carry a level shift of about 14 %.
vulcan.model:
Model and inversion

Mesh           75 x 75 x 164 cells; core 45 x 45 cells of 250 m; layers from
               5 m at the top; base at 50 km
Position       UTM zone 53 south, WGS84; mesh rotated 0.2 degrees
               anticlockwise; model top at +125 m
Values         resistivity in ohm.m (2.5 to 1280); air cells are 1e10
Software       CGG RLM-3D V1.2.7, run from Geotools 3.0.1
Run            June 2022, 40 iterations, final nRMS 0.96
Data           full impedance tensor, no tipper; 98 of the 100 Level 2
               sites (B8 and I3 not used); 17 frequencies, 100 to 0.01 Hz
Error floors   10 % on Zxx and Zyy, 2 % on Zxy and Zyx
Distortion     a real 2 x 2 matrix solved for at each site
Start model    uniform 100 ohm.m
Bounds         0.5 to 5000 ohm.m

Contents of the package

inputs/
  EDI_input/        impedances as given to the inversion (98 sites)
  EDI_used/         the same, with the error floors applied
  sites.csv         site, easting, northing, elevation (UTM 53S, m)
  freq.dat          the 17 frequencies (Hz)
  Job_RLM3DMT_4_parameters.txt    all inversion settings
  Vulcan_Default_start.out        start model, uniform 100 ohm.m

outputs/
  model/            final model with its padding cells, for computing:
                    .out (native WinGLink / RLM-3D format), .msh and
                    .mod (UBC; see limit 2).
                    The same model without padding, for viewing only:
                    _trimmed.vtk (VTK structured grid; air cells are
                    nan) and _trimmed.xyzv (easting, northing,
                    elevation, ohm.m; no air cells). These keep the
                    core, 5 cells on each side and the top 134
                    layers: 17.1 x 17.1 km, to 20.4 km below the
                    model top. Being inside this block does not
                    mean a cell is resolved by the data.
  responses/        predicted impedances with and without the distortion
                    matrices; the distortion matrices
  misfit/           nRMS by iteration, site, frequency and component
  figures/          depth slices, sections, nRMS against iteration

File names are those of the inversion run: "Vulcan4" and "Job_RLM3DMT_4"
mean this model.

sunda.title: Bridging the gap between subduction dynamics and the long-term strength of the Sunda megathrust
sunda.snapshot:
Subduction zone forces strongly influence tectonic stresses and earthquake behaviour along convergent margins. In the Sunda region (Java–Sumatra–Andaman), variations in slab pull and mantle flow control how plates move and interact. Using high-resolution 3-D models that match present-day observations, we show that the pull of the Java slab dominates regional dynamics, driving northward-increasing oblique convergence, trench advance near Sumatra, and stronger plate coupling. The modelled stress patterns agree with geodetic data and earthquake stress orientations. Frictional strength variations along the megathrust identify key depth zones that align with major earthquake locations, highlighting how deep subduction processes set conditions for seismic events.

a) Mantle flow at 300 km depth in Model 1. Arrows for horizontal flow velocities, in color for the vertical velocity. b) Mantle flow streamlines, in color for the vertical velocity. Positive vertical velocities represent mantle upwelling, whereas negative vertical velocities indicate mantle downwelling. In dark green the subducting lithosphere and blue for the subducting slab. Lower mantle in light green. a) was created with open-source software Python and library Matplotlib, b) with open-source software Paraview.
sunda.overview:
Research Tags

Subduction stresses sunda earthquake

Associated Publication

Bridging the gap between subduction dynamics and the long-term strength of the Sunda megathrust
Fabio A. Capitanio, Thyagarajulu Gollapalli, Radhakrishna Munukutla, Juan Carlos Graciosa, Zuhair Mohd, Adam Beall, Luca Dal Zilio
Pub. DOI10.1038/s41467-025-65824-7

Abstract

The link between great earthquakes and subduction dynamics across a wide range of scales remains a crucial, yet elusive, tenet of the seismotectonics of convergent margins. Here, we show high-performance computational simulations of the three-dimensional Sunda subduction zone dynamics matching plate motions, tectonics and current deformation, thereby providing insights into the stress regime of the Java-Sumatra-Andaman margin. Testing various tectonic forces reveals the primary control of the Java slab pull and induced mantle flow on the whole margin tectonics, driving northward-increasing oblique convergence, Sumatran trench advance and increased tectonic coupling along this segment. The modelled deviatoric stresses reproduce the geodetically-constrained interseismic compression in Sumatra and megathrust stress orientations notably consistent with the seismic P-axes, with magnitude comparable to static stresses on seismogenic faults. We map the frictional strength along the Sumatra-Andaman megathrust, identifying critical thresholds at key seismogenic depths, which remarkably correlate with the location of great earthquakes. Our outcomes show how subduction dynamics may critically prime the conditions for seismicity along the Sunda margin.
sunda.model:
Model data storage

Software

Software: underworldcode/underworld2: v2.8.1b
Software DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.3384283

Model Input Notes

We model subduction in a regional spherical domain using Stokes flow of an incompressible fluid with an infinite Prandtl number. The Southeast Asian subduction zone is simulated within a portion of a spherical shell. The domain is discretised with a uniform mesh in longitude and latitude, and a non-uniform mesh in the radial direction, resulting in element sizes of ~15×15×10 km in the upper mantle and ~15×15×37 km in the lower mantle. Each element contains 20 Lagrangian particles to track material properties and improve resolution of stress variations. All model boundaries are assigned free-slip conditions.

Model Setup

Setup of Model 1, 2 and 3. The models consist of a subducting plate with an attached slab, upper plate, upper mantle, and lower mantle. The mantle depth is 1000 km in (A) and (B), and 2891 km in (C). The thickness of the upper plate is 90 km in all models. The line with open squares indicates the trace of the interface.

detachment.title: Kinematics of Footwall Exhumation at Oceanic Detachment faults: Solid‐Block Rotation and Apparent Unbending
detachment.snapshot:
This model was developed in order to study the rotation of footwall rocks beneath oceanic detachment faults (ODFs). It showed that solid-block rotation dominates beneath a concave-down fault, while significant flexural stresses form later during apparent unbending, causing both compression and extension-related brittle strain within oceanic core complexes (OCCs).

Animation showing alternative model (see paper for detail). Colormap shows vorticity/rotation rate. Velocity vectors are shown in the hangingwall reference frame. Dark regions show the acccumulation of plastic strain.
detachment.overview:
Research Tags

tectonics faulting detachment faults

Associated Publication

Kinematics of Footwall Exhumation at Oceanic Detachment faults: Solid‐Block Rotation and Apparent Unbending
Dan Sandiford, Sascha Brune, Anne Glerum, John Naliboff, Joanne M. Whittaker
Pub. DOI10.1029/2021gc009681

Abstract

Seafloor spreading at slow rates can be accommodated on large‐offset oceanic detachment faults (ODFs), that exhume lower crustal and mantle rocks in footwall domes termed oceanic core complexes (OCCs). Footwall rocks experience large rotation during exhumation, yet important aspects of the kinematics—particularly the relative roles of solid‐block rotation and flexure—are not clearly understood. Using a high‐resolution numerical model, we explore the exhumation kinematics in the footwall beneath an emergent ODF/OCC. A key feature of the models is that footwall motion is dominated by solid‐block rotation, accommodated by the nonplanar, concave‐down fault interface. A consequence is that curvature measured along the ODF is representative of a neutral stress configuration, rather than a “bent” one. Instead, it is in the subsequent process of “apparent unbending” that significant flexural stresses are developed in the model footwall. The brittle strain associated with apparent unbending is produced dominantly in extension, beneath the OCC, consistent with earthquake clustering observed in the Trans‐Atlantic Geotraverse at the Mid‐Atlantic Ridge.
detachment.model:
Model data storage

Software

Software: geodynamics/aspect: ASPECT 2.5.0
Software DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.8200213

Model Links

https://github.com/dansand/odf_paper

Model Input Notes

ASPECT Input files for model. Input file has been updated for compatibility with more recent ASPECT versions. Input file tested on ASPECT version 2.6.0-pre (fix_stresses_elasticity, 621dd61f2), using deal.II 9.4.2.

Model Setup

Initial conditions, showing mesh refinement.

Model Output Notes

Data directory contains output data for 2 simulations stored in the following directories: ref_model_hires, alt_model_hires. Top level contains typical ASPECT output files, including log.txt and restart files. Topography and mesh variables were output at 100 Kyr intervals. Model end time is 5 Myr. Main output data consists of of plain text files representing model topography (e.g. topography.00000), vtu files (in the ./solution sub-directory) representing model output fields (e.g. solution-00000.0000.vtu). At each output step, there are 16 vtu files written. These can be opened with Paraview using the solution.pvd file in the top level.
